The system was isolated and upgraded, and the audit closed.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Head of IT at a financial institution

stories.text: We gave our admin login an unguessable address and then published that address in the rules file. Automated attacks against it began the same week, with no scanning beforehand  we had handed over the map. sus.bot rated the line a high-severity disclosure. Proper protections went on the login and the address came out of the file, and the attacks lost their target.

The first page of our client's penetration test report cited their rules file for naming the back-office address. The tester needed no scanning at all: read the file, open the address, find an unprotected login. sus.bot had flagged the identical issue in a report we'd filed away without action. The path was renamed, throttled and removed before the retest  this time with management's full attention.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Development manager at a chemicals supplier

stories.text: A rule copied from a tutorial hid our system's diagnostic pages from search  while the pages themselves stayed completely open to anyone. One of them printed configuration details, including the production database password, to anyone who asked. sus.bot flagged the rule as a disclosure rather than a protection. Passwords rotated, pages locked down, rule deleted, and a very awkward customer conversation avoided.

A backup folder named in the file still allowed browsing on the server, and a complete copy of our database  every order, every password  sat two clicks away. The first people to notice were a bug bounty hunter, not any of our own tools. sus.bot treats such paths as worth checking. The dump was destroyed, browsing was disabled, and the folder no longer exists.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Managing director at a parts supplier

stories.text: We blocked common archive types from search, and an automated scanner read those two rules as a shopping list: it guessed the obvious filename, requested it, and received a database dump from a migration nobody remembered running. sus.bot treats those extensions in rules as advertised targets. The dump was deleted, the forgotten server decommissioned, and the lines removed.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Data protection officer at an insurer

stories.text: Customer invoices were kept out of search with a rule instead of out of the internet with a login. Invoice numbers ran in sequence, so one customer edited the number in her URL and read a stranger's invoice  then reported us, starting a formal notification process that took longer than the fix itself. sus.bot had already flagged the folder as sensitive content hiding behind a signpost. Authentication went on the next day.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Retail director at a supermarket chain

stories.text: An installation routine stayed reachable a full year after launch, and our rules file pointed straight at it. Someone ran it, redirected our site to their own setup, and collected customer passwords on the fake login for two days before a shopper noticed the branding looked wrong. sus.bot classified the path as critical on its first run. The routine was deleted, and customers were told before the press could tell them.

A rushed deploy added a rule for our code-history folder  which was the first sign it was being served to the world at all. The entire history was fetchable, including a change meant to remove an API key, which merely preserved it. We spent a weekend rotating every credential. sus.bot had flagged the line as exposure of a sensitive folder. Access is now blocked at the server, and the rule is gone.

A rule named our configuration file and I believed the file was therefore protected. A rule only keeps things out of search results  it stops nobody. Our mail credentials were used to send phishing from our own domain, and the mail provider told us before our own monitoring did. sus.bot's severity note says it exactly: the line is a signpost, not a lock. The file was moved out of reach that afternoon.

I assumed a rule for an ancient scripts folder was leftover decoration from an old template. It was a live map: a form handler from a previous agency's era still answered there, with a security flaw old enough to have grandchildren. sus.bot flagged the path as legacy surface worth probing. The handler was deleted, the folder removed, and the rule retired with it.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Operations director at an import company

stories.text: A colleague blocked our test site's paths from the live site, hoping to keep the copy out of search. The test site had its own permissive rules, so it stayed visible anyway  and our rule told every reader that a twin existed, complete with a restored customer database. sus.bot flagged both the useless rule and the unprotected twin. A login went onto the test site, and the rule came out.

A rule for our redesign folder went live three weeks before the redesign did. A trade journalist read the file, browsed the folder, and published our new pricing tiers ahead of the announcement. Nothing was broken  the file simply answered a question nobody had asked yet. sus.bot flagged the pre-launch path as an early announcement. Future sections go in at launch, not before.

The client insisted their software version was confidential, while their rules file pointed at a changelog naming the exact release. A public exploit for that release had been circulating for months before our audit. sus.bot flagged the referenced file as a version disclosure. The changelog left the web, the rule was deleted, and the confidentiality they cared about was finally real.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Digital manager at a bakery chain

stories.text: Following a security recommendation we blocked a folder of website code, and within three weeks the usability reports showed our navigation as broken  search engines were judging a version of our site with no menu on it. sus.bot's rendering check failed the same week and linked the block to the breakage directly. Reopening the folder restored the layout, and mobile performance recovered.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: SEO lead at a fitness company

stories.text: The search engine's snapshot of our homepage became a single grey column of unstyled text. I spent two quarters blaming the template and redesigning around a problem one blocked folder had caused. sus.bot's rendering check named the blocked stylesheet in its failure detail. The preview that needed hiding moved behind a URL parameter, and the snapshots returned to normal.

One capital letter meant our admin rule matched nothing, and our login page turned up in a search for our company name. The rule had never blocked a single request in its life. sus.bot flagged the capitalisation mismatch on its first scan. One lower-case edit later, the login was covered and the embarrassing result cleared.

Our shop answered both the capitalised and lower-case versions of a category address. The rule covered only the capitalised one, so half the duplicate pages were blocked and the other half were indexed  the worst possible split, and our reporting couldn't explain it. sus.bot matched the rules against both spellings and showed the uncovered half in a table. We fixed the addresses first, then one rule covered everything.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Sales director at a hardware vendor

stories.text: A rule meant to keep source maps private also swept up the code that renders our product prices, and prices vanished from the search listings we had spent a quarter winning. Customers called asking if we'd gone out of stock. sus.bot flagged the rule as blocking something the site needs to display. Narrowing it to the map files brought the prices back within two weeks.

A client's file blocked every stylesheet on the domain, a rule that survived four redesigns because their own browser always looked perfect. What search engines rendered had no layout at all, and the mobile index judged that version of the site. sus.bot's rendered snapshot of a blocked page ended the argument in one meeting. The rule was removed and mobile visibility recovered.

A plugin kept rules at the top of the file while a colleague hand-maintained a second copy at the bottom. I edited the bottom copy to open a folder, saw no change, and wasted a week before discovering the top block had been in charge the whole time. sus.bot shows both blocks and their overlap on one screen. The duplicate copy was deleted, and the file has exactly one owner now.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: E-commerce director at an interiors retailer

stories.text: To discourage a photo thief we blocked our entire image folder. Image search traffic collapsed within a month, and the thief, who never reads rules, took the photos anyway. We lost a marketing channel and deterred nobody. sus.bot flagged the block as pure self-harm. We lifted it, watermarked the images, and the traffic returned.

A rule from an old migration covered the folder holding all our recipe photography. The articles still ranked, but with no picture beside them  and nobody ever files a ticket about a missing thumbnail, so it stood unchallenged for years. sus.bot listed the blocked image folder as a pure ranking loss. Removing the line restored the thumbnails on the next image crawl.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Head of e-commerce at a nursery retailer

stories.text: Two teams each added their own general section to the file, and each section read perfectly on its own. Search engines combine them, and the combination blocked our newly launched section completely  the launch numbers made no sense for weeks. sus.bot shows the combined result before anything ships, which explained the launch in one screen. Consolidating the sections got the new range indexed within days.

A leftover line from an old test sat under the rule protecting our pricing pages, and by the file's own tie-breaking rules, the leftover won. Our pricing sheets stayed visible to search for a year while the file read as though they were closed. sus.bot evaluates the rules the way engines do and marks the winner. Deleting one stale line closed the folder, confirmed by the next scan.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Content manager at a media group

stories.text: I opened our documentation folder to search and waited for the manuals to appear. An old rule above mine, one character longer, beat it for every single page  the file has a longest-rule-wins grammar nobody had explained to me. sus.bot's view shows the winning rule per page at a glance. One deleted line, and the manuals were indexed within the week.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Head of e-commerce at a furniture retailer

stories.text: One rule intended to collapse duplicate tracking addresses also swallowed every filtered colour and size combination we sell. Half our catalogue existed only behind those filters, so half our catalogue effectively vanished from search overnight. sus.bot showed the rule matching every filtered page in a table nobody could argue with. Restricting it to the tracking parameter restored the catalogue in three weeks.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Operations manager at a supplies wholesaler

stories.text: The file carried eleven detailed rules plus one simple rule that covered everything. A rewrite dropped the simple one, and whoever approved it saw the eleven and assumed coverage; three folders nobody had listed went into search. sus.bot flags the redundancy and the resulting gap in the same report. The simple rule came back, and the eleven were simplified away.

A broad rule meant for text exports matched our rules file itself, along with our terms page and three support downloads. Customers started reporting dead download links before we understood why. sus.bot's check pointed directly at the rule covering the file's own address. Tightening it freed the file and every download in a single edit.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Marketing lead at an online shop

stories.text: While our new checkout was being built we blocked a shop path and forgot one character. Rules work as prefixes, so our best landing page  whose address merely started with the same letters  went with it, and four months of traffic quietly disappeared. sus.bot lists every address a rule matches, which made the collateral damage obvious. The character went in, and traffic recovered over the following quarter.

The client insisted their rule covered one folder. It covered eleven, because a rule matches everything sharing its beginning. We settled the debate by reading the eleven matches aloud in a meeting. sus.bot prints the same list in its report, which ended the argument faster than I did. The rule got its character, and ten innocent folders were released.

A sitemap service hosted our catalogue on their own domain and told us it was all connected. The search console showed no submissions at all, because our site was never verified against their domain  and thousands of pages sat undiscovered for a quarter while we paid for a service that wasn't connected to anything. sus.bot flagged the cross-domain pointer. Self-hosting fixed it, and the pages were found within the week.

Two systems each declared the same catalogue, so I removed one, and the next update put it back; I removed the other, and we ended up with no catalogue declared at all for three weeks. sus.bot's change history showed both systems writing the same line, which made the tug of war visible. The declaration moved into our template, and both systems' output was switched off.

Our catalogue pointer promised a secure address our website couldn't actually serve  the certificate behind it had expired a year earlier. Every attempt to read the catalogue failed silently while the line looked perfectly current to anyone reviewing it. sus.bot fetches the address exactly as written and reported the failure. Correcting it restored discovery the same day, and the security update finally got scheduled.

author.name: Anonymous
author.role: Digital director at an interiors retailer

stories.text: Our catalogue lives on a separate service, and the one line connecting it to our shop was lost when a template regenerated the file. The catalogue kept reporting 'all fine' while covering nothing at all  the worst way to fail, because nothing looked broken. sus.bot caught the missing line in its change review. Restoring it reconnected the catalogue within the hour.

Two years after moving to a secure website, our catalogue pointer still named the old insecure address. Every read crossed a detour, and the reports showed an address nobody could match to anything we produced, which made every conversation about search performance needlessly mysterious. sus.bot flagged the mismatch and the detour. One update later, the reports finally showed our own address.
